Seal projects to OS accounts

peer_auth - one daemon, a Unix socket that names each caller by its uid, projects only their own OS account can reach, and the deployment that makes the files hold too.

On this page
  • How it decides
  • Configure it
  • Deploy it: the daemon runs as its own account
  • Connect the owner
  • Connect a sealed account's agents
  • Verify
  • Move an existing install over
  • Roll back
  • What changes with peer_auth on

Project isolation keeps agents working on one project out of another's knowledge. It is a policy fence: it trusts the session binding an agent reports, every caller shares one bearer key, and the corpus is files in your home directory that any process of yours can read.

peer_auth is the boundary underneath it, for when the threat is an account rather than a stray agent: you run a sensitive system's agents under their own macOS or Linux user, and nothing running as you - no agent, no script, no tool - may read that system's memory, through Seamless or through a file. One daemon serves everyone. It identifies each caller by the uid the kernel reports for its Unix-socket connection, never by anything the caller sends, and it maps OS accounts to the projects they may reach.

It is off by default, and off means exactly the behavior every release before it had. It also asks for a different deployment: the daemon has to run as an account of its own, or the files would not hold.

How it decides

Every request carries a principal, set by the transport before any route runs:

Connection Principal
TCP with the bearer key the owner account (peer_auth.owner)
The socket, from the owner's uid the owner
The socket, from a uid listed under peer_auth.users that account
The socket, from any other uid refused with 403 before any route runs

Two rules follow, and they are the whole policy:

  1. A project sealed to an account is reachable only from that account's socket connections. The owner - TCP key and socket alike - never reaches it.
  2. A configured account reaches only its own projects (the ones sealed to it plus any it shares), and it reads the global scope but never writes it: a global memory is injected into every project's briefing, the owner's included.
A project sealed to this account Sealed to another account The owner's projects Global, read Global, write
Owner - no yes yes yes
Configured account yes no only if listed under projects yes no

"Reach" means everything: recall, briefings, the prompt matcher, every MCP tool by name or by id, tasks, trials, sessions, the gardener's proposals, the hooks, A2A, the console and its live feed. A project an account may not reach is simply absent from what it lists, and a call that names one is refused with the rule and the remedy, never with any of its content.

A configured account works in its own projects whatever its working directory: its sessions, and any call nothing else places, land in its home project - its first sealed project, else its first shared one. It never grows the repo map. The owner opening a repository whose project is sealed to another account gets a one-line notice in place of a briefing, and no session.

The console belongs to the owner: a configured account gets 403, and the owner's console shows no project sealed to another account - not in a list, a count's detail, a search, a chart, the event log or the live feed.

Sealing works with isolation rather than replacing it: every sealed project must also be confidential or sealed, which keeps it standalone (no family, no parent) and inside the existing fences between agents.

Configure it

peer_auth:
  enabled: true
  owner: alice                      # the account the TCP bearer key stands for
  socket:
    path: /opt/seamless/run/seamlessd.sock
    mode: "0666"                    # who may knock; the kernel still names each one
  users:
    _payroll:                       # an OS user name, or a numeric uid
      sealed: [payroll]             # reachable only from _payroll
    _ops_bot:
      projects: [ops]               # shared: _ops_bot and the owner both reach it

Checked when the file loads. The users map always, whether or not enabled is set: a project sealed to two accounts, a project sealed to one account and listed for another, a project listed twice for one account, the global scope or the reserved all listed, and an account reaching nothing. With enabled set, also: the owner is named and not listed under users, the socket path is absolute and outside data_dir, and the mode is octal and keeps owner read and write.

Checked when serve starts, and refused if any fails:

  • every account resolves on this machine (macOS role accounts live in the directory service, and are found there), and no two entries share a uid;
  • every project the block names exists - a misspelled seal would leave the project it meant open, which is exactly what this feature exists to prevent;
  • every sealed project is confidential or sealed;
  • the files would hold too (the next section).

seamlessd doctor, run as the daemon's account against the daemon's config, prints the policy as it resolved and every reason serve would refuse.

Deploy it: the daemon runs as its own account

The data directory holds every project's memory in plain files and a SQLite database. If the daemon runs as you, every process of yours reads them. So with peer_auth on, serve refuses to start unless:

  • it runs as neither the owner nor root;
  • data_dir belongs to the daemon's account and is mode 0700;
  • the socket's directory belongs to the daemon's account or root and is not group- or world-writable (whoever can write it can replace the socket and impersonate the daemon to every caller);
  • every directory above the data, the socket, the config file and the binary belongs to root or the daemon's account and is not writable by anyone else - a directory you own anywhere above the data is one you can rename it out of;
  • the config file and the seamlessd binary belong to root or the daemon's account and are not group- or world-writable: whoever can rewrite either can switch the boundary off at the next start.

A layout that satisfies all of it (macOS shown; Linux is the same with useradd --system and a systemd unit):

Path Owner Mode Holds
/opt/seamless root:wheel 0755
/opt/seamless/bin root:wheel 0755 seamlessd, seam (both 0755, root's)
/opt/seamless/etc root:wheel 0755 seamless.yaml (root:_seamless, 0640)
/opt/seamless/data _seamless 0700 the database and corpus
/opt/seamless/run _seamless 0755 the socket
/opt/seamless/home _seamless 0700 the account's home (caches, nothing else)

Create the account (macOS, as an administrator; pick an unused uid in the role range - dscl . -list /Users UniqueID lists the taken ones):

sudo dscl . -create /Groups/_seamless PrimaryGroupID 480
sudo dscl . -create /Users/_seamless UniqueID 480
sudo dscl . -create /Users/_seamless PrimaryGroupID 480
sudo dscl . -create /Users/_seamless UserShell /usr/bin/false
sudo dscl . -create /Users/_seamless NFSHomeDirectory /opt/seamless/home
sudo dscl . -create /Users/_seamless Password '*'
sudo dscl . -create /Users/_seamless IsHidden 1

The service is a LaunchDaemon that names the account (on Linux, a system unit with User=), so it runs whether or not anyone is logged in. The plist, its controls, and how to retire the per-user service first are in the service reference.

Connect the owner

Nothing changes for the owner's agents. They keep the TCP listener and the bearer key, and they are the owner: every project except the sealed ones. Their config becomes a client's, because the owner's account no longer runs the daemon - and a server-role config there would have seamlessd doctor open (and create) a database in the owner's home:

role: client
server_url: "http://127.0.0.1:8081"
mcp:
  api_key: "<the same key as the daemon's config>"

The owner can use the socket instead (server_url: unix:///opt/seamless/run/seamlessd.sock, no key): same principal, no key on disk. The console still needs TCP - a browser cannot dial a socket.

Connect a sealed account's agents

An agent for a sealed system runs as that system's account. That is also how a person works on the system with its memory: they run the session as the account, with sudo -u, and their own account's sessions cannot reach it.

The account's config, in its own home (~/.config/seamless/seamless.yaml, mode 0600):

role: client
server_url: "unix:///opt/seamless/run/seamlessd.sock"

No key: the daemon names the caller by its uid. Then install its hooks and MCP registration, as the account:

sudo -u _payroll -H /opt/seamless/bin/seamlessd install-hooks --client claude \
  --seam /opt/seamless/bin/seam

With a socket server_url every hook is a seam hook <event> command (Claude Code's own http hook cannot dial a socket) and the MCP registration is the seam mcp-proxy stdio bridge. If you write them by hand, the account's ~/.claude/settings.json hook entries look like:

{"type": "command", "command": "/opt/seamless/bin/seam",
 "args": ["hook", "session-start", "--config", "/home/of/_payroll/.config/seamless/seamless.yaml"]}

one per event (session-start, user-prompt-submit, session-end, post-tool-use, subagent-start, subagent-stop, permission-request), and its ~/.claude.json MCP server is:

"seamless": {"type": "stdio", "command": "/opt/seamless/bin/seam",
             "args": ["mcp-proxy", "--config", "/home/of/_payroll/.config/seamless/seamless.yaml"]}

Then run the session as the account: sudo -u _payroll -H claude. The account needs its own Claude Code sign-in, and its own copy of anything the session reads - it cannot traverse your home directory, which is the point.

Verify

# As root or the daemon's account: the policy, and nothing serve would refuse.
sudo -u _seamless env SEAMLESS_CONFIG=/opt/seamless/etc/seamless.yaml /opt/seamless/bin/seamlessd doctor

# As the owner: the files are out of reach, and so is the sealed project.
ls /opt/seamless/data                         # Permission denied
seam recall something --project payroll      # refused: not reachable from this connection

# As the sealed account: its own project, and the global scope.
sudo -u _payroll -H /opt/seamless/bin/seam doctor
sudo -u _payroll -H /opt/seamless/bin/seam recall something

# As any other account: refused at the door.
curl --unix-socket /opt/seamless/run/seamlessd.sock http://localhost/healthz   # 403

Move an existing install over

The data directory moves as a whole; the database stores paths relative to it, so nothing inside needs rewriting. On one volume the move is a rename.

  1. Seal first, in the old world. Make each sealed project confidential or sealed (seam project isolation <slug> confidential --yes) and run seamlessd doctor with the new config to catch a misspelled slug.
  2. Back up, as the owner, while the old daemon still serves: seamlessd export -o ~/seamless-before-peer-auth.tar.gz. The archive holds every project, the sealed ones included - keep it where the sealed accounts' data would be kept.
  3. Create the account and the layout above, and install root-owned copies of both binaries in /opt/seamless/bin.
  4. Write the daemon's config at /opt/seamless/etc/seamless.yaml (root:_seamless 0640): the owner's old config with data_dir: /opt/seamless/data, the peer_auth block, and the same mcp.api_key and LLM keys.
  5. Stop the old service and move the data: stop and remove the per-user service (how), then sudo mv ~/.seamless /opt/seamless/data, sudo chown -R _seamless:_seamless /opt/seamless/data and sudo chmod -R go-rwx /opt/seamless/data.
  6. Start the daemon: install and load the LaunchDaemon, then curl -s http://127.0.0.1:8081/healthz and the doctor line above.
  7. Switch the owner's config to the client config above.
  8. Wire each sealed account as described above, and verify.

Roll back

Unload the LaunchDaemon (how), move the data back (sudo mv /opt/seamless/data ~/.seamless and sudo chown -R $(id -un):staff ~/.seamless), restore the owner's server config without the peer_auth block - a release that predates it refuses the key - and reinstall the per-user service (make install, or the installer). The export from step 2 is the fallback if anything in the move went wrong.

What changes with peer_auth on

  • The daemon reads no agent files. Session-end findings and token totals harvested from transcripts, model sniffing, and plan-file and subagent capture are off: under peer_auth every path a hook names is one some other account chose, and the daemon can read its own data directory, so honoring one could make it read a sealed project's files on a caller's behalf. Agents still record findings with session_end. (The daemon could not read your transcripts anyway: it no longer runs as you.)
  • Updates are an administrator's step. A LaunchDaemon install is not one the installer made, so the daemon only notifies; replace /opt/seamless/bin with sudo and restart it. Run make install only with a client-role config, so it updates your own seam and hooks and leaves the service alone.
  • Counts stay machine-wide in usage_summary, as they are for isolation: volume, never content, and the same number for every caller.
  • The boundary is the OS account. Root, and anyone who can become the daemon's account or a sealed account, reads everything; passwordless sudo voids the whole arrangement. Whoever holds the bearer key acts as the owner (which reaches no seal). Backups of the data directory, and exports, hold every project - treat them as the most sealed thing in them.
  • The gardener still runs over every project, as the daemon, for no caller. Its proposals about a sealed project reach only that account's agents (gardener_proposals); the owner's console does not show them.
